title: Chore Chart Template: Free, Editable & Printable
meta_description: Free chore chart template you can edit online and print, no account needed. A dad of four shares how to build a template you'll actually keep using.
h1: Chore Chart Template (Free, Editable Online, Printable)
intro: Most people searching for a chore chart template want the same thing: a clean starting grid they can make their own in a couple of minutes, not a locked PDF they have to fight with. That's exactly what this page hands you. Use the format picker just below to start from a blank template and edit it right in your browser, type in your own names and jobs, pick daily or weekly, and print it without making an account or handing over an email. Under the picker you'll find a linked map of every template and format we've built, from blank grids to weekly and daily layouts to age-specific versions. I'm Andrew, writing for the SproutChores family. We're raising four kids of our own, currently nine through eighteen, and over the years we've also fostered a few younger ones who showed up with no routine at all. We've filled out a lot of these grids, and we built the editor here to be the part that's usually missing from a free template: a real one you can change, not just a picture you download. So start a template above, then read on for how to shape it into something your family will still be using a month from now.

sections.heading: What a good chore chart template actually needs
sections.body:
A template is just a starting frame, and the best one is the one you'll bother to keep. After years of doing this, we've found the frame matters less than how easy it is to change and to restart. Three things make the difference for us.

First, it has to be genuinely editable. A lot of what shows up under a search like this is a fixed image or a one-size grid you can't really adjust, which is why people end up asking for a Google Docs, Sheets, or Excel version they can finally type into. The editor above skips that step: you change the names, swap the jobs, and add or drop rows right here before you print. The goal is your house on the page, not someone else's idea of a tidy week.

Second, it should be short enough to win. The most common mistake we see is a beautiful, packed grid that looks impressive and gets ignored by Friday. A child who finishes a small list every day builds more than one who learns to tune out a long one. Start lean, leave room, and let the template grow as your kid does.

Third, and least obvious, it has to be cheap and quick to put back up. Real family life knocks any system sideways eventually, a holiday, a sick week, a stretch of chaos. The templates that last in our house aren't the elaborate ones; they're the ones we can reprint and pin back on the fridge in two minutes after everything falls apart. So when you customize yours, keep it simple enough that restarting it never feels like a project.

sections.heading: Edit online or download to Google Docs, Sheets, or Excel?
sections.body:
This is the fork most people hit, and the honest answer depends on what you're after. If you want to tweak the template once and be done, editing it here and printing it on the spot is the fastest path, and it leaves nothing to set up. If you genuinely want to keep rebuilding it from scratch every season, a spreadsheet you own can make sense, but be honest with yourself about whether you'll actually maintain it.

We spent a while trying to be the parents who ran the whole house from a phone or a shared doc, and it quietly fell apart for one plain reason: a file lives where the grown-ups look, and no child ever opens it. A chart only changes anything when the kid can glance at it and know what's next without being told. That's the case for printing whatever template you choose and sticking it somewhere they walk past, rather than leaving it in a tab.

So our take is simple. Use the editor to shape the template to your family, print the version you land on, and put it where the work happens. The format you choose, blank, weekly, or daily, is linked below; pick the one that matches the problem you're actually solving, not the one that looks cutest. A template you'll see every day beats a sophisticated file nobody opens.

sections.heading: The template is a tool for you, not a bribe for them
sections.body:
Here's the piece we feel most strongly about, because it shapes how you should fill the grid in. A chore chart template is a tracking tool for parents. It's how you see at a glance who's keeping up and who needs a hand, not a machine for getting kids to behave. We keep the motivation off the chart on purpose.

That means we don't price the boxes. We never pay our kids square by square, because that turns helping your own family into a transaction. The everyday jobs belong to the household, and we say so out loud, the contribution is the point. Allowance does exist in our house, but it rides on the bigger picture of effort, reliability, and the attitude a kid brings, not on a per-task tally. We also keep screen time and treats out of the chart entirely, so cooperation never curdles into a negotiation over what they'll get for it.

We learned how much that structure matters while fostering. The little ones who came to us had lived with no predictable rhythm, and a small, dependable routine they could count on did far more for them than any reward we could have dangled. Once they trusted what came next, a lot of what we'd assumed was defiance turned out to be them simply not knowing. The same holds for any kid, and it's the real reason we frame these templates the way we do: chores aren't about getting the house clean. They're rehearsal for running a life, and the chart is just how we keep track of the practice.

faq.q: Is this chore chart template really free, and can I edit it?
faq.a: Yes on both counts. You can start from a blank template, edit it right in your browser, type in your own names and jobs, and print it, with no account to create and no email to hand over. Nothing here is locked behind a paid tier. Use the picker above to choose a format, customize the grid to fit your family, and print it straight to your home printer.

faq.q: Should I use the online editor or a Google Docs or Excel template?
faq.a: If you want to tweak the template and have it ready in a couple of minutes, editing it here and printing it is the quickest route, with nothing to set up. A spreadsheet you own can suit people who genuinely plan to rebuild the chart from scratch each season, but be honest about whether you'll keep that up. Whichever you pick, print it and put it where your kids actually walk past, because a chart only works when they can see it.

faq.q: Is there one chore chart template that works for every age?
faq.a: Not really. The template is just the frame; what you put in it should match where your child actually is. Start lean, with a short list a younger kid can finish every day, and add to it as they prove they can carry more. We've built age-specific versions, linked below, so you can start from a template already shaped for that stage instead of guessing. Treat any starting point as a default you adjust up or down to fit your specific kid.
